findings.severity_note: Raised to critical: rated high and backed by advertising or session-replay evidence.
findings.title: Advertising identifier conflicts with the policy's anonymity claim
findings.detail: A unique _ga identifier was sent to Google advertising domains before any consent choice, while the policy describes the relevant cookies as anonymous and says the information cannot identify the user.
findings.law: PECR reg. 6; UK GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 13
findings.policy_quote: The cookies collect information in an anonymous form, including the number of visitors to the site, where visitors have come to the site from and the pages they visited. This information cannot be used to identify who you are.
findings.reasoning: The observed unique identifier was sent to advertising-related Google domains, which is inconsistent with the policy's description of anonymous analytics information. This is high severity because it is a direct transparency and fairness contradiction alongside evidence of pre-consent advertising tracking.
findings.law_eu: ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC Art. 5(3) (consent before storing/reading on a device); EU GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 13

findings.title: Google cookies were set before you could choose
findings.detail: 2 tracking cookies (_ga, _ga_5RDX1YK9YG) were already set before the cookie banner was answered (Advertising). _ga, _ga_5RDX1YK9YG hold what looks like a unique ID.
findings.law: PECR reg. 6 (consent needed before storing cookies)
findings.law_eu: ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC Art. 5(3) (consent before storing/reading on a device)

findings.title: Your ID was sent to Google before you answered the cookie banner
findings.detail: The value of _ga (an ID unique to this browser) was sent to doubleclick.net, google.co.uk in the request address. This lets Google recognise this browser on later visits.
findings.law: PECR reg. 6 (reading an identifier stored on your device and sending it on is 'access' and needs consent); UK GDPR Art. 4(1) (an online identifier is personal data)
findings.law_eu: ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC Art. 5(3) (consent before storing/reading on a device); EU GDPR Art. 4(1)

findings.title: 1 tracking company not named in the privacy policy
findings.detail: The policy names 3 companies. We saw these and found no mention: Microsoft. (The policy may describe them only by category, e.g. 'advertising partners'.)
findings.law: UK GDPR Art. 13(1)(e) (you must be told who receives your data)

findings.title: International transfer information is incomplete
findings.detail: The policy says Google stores cookie information on servers in the United States, while the audit observed an identifier being sent to Google before consent. The policy does not explain the transfer safeguard or other legal mechanism relied on for the international transfer.
findings.reasoning: The policy provides some location information, so this is not a complete absence of disclosure. However, it does not identify the Article 44 transfer mechanism or safeguards; severity is medium because the evidence and policy do not establish whether a lawful transfer arrangement exists.

findings.title: Privacy policy is missing 2 required items
findings.detail: Not covered anywhere in the policy we read: Who is responsible (the controller); Right to complain to the ICO.
findings.law: UK GDPR Art. 13(1)-(2) (information that must be given to people)
findings.reasoning: Checked against the Art. 13 list. Each item marked missing was reported missing by the AI review AND has no matching keywords anywhere in the full policy text.

findings.title: Accept is one click, but we found no way to reject
findings.detail: The banner offers "Privacy Policy & Cookies", but our automated check could not find any reject or decline option. (This may be a limit of our check, so treat it as something to verify.)
findings.law: ICO cookie guidance (refusing must be as easy as accepting)
findings.law_eu: EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 on consent; EDPB Cookie Banner Taskforce report (2023)

letter.subject: Concern regarding cookies, tracking and privacy information on babcockinternational.com
letter.body:
Dear Data Protection Officer,

I am writing to raise concerns identified during an automated, passive audit of https://babcockinternational.com on 2026-11-08 04:14 UTC. The audit used a fresh browser session and recorded what cookies and network requests were present before any consent choice. No cookie banner was found, so no reject option could be clicked.

The audit found the following issues which I ask you to explain:

1. Two Google tracking cookies, _ga and _ga_5RDX1YK9YG, were already set before any cookie banner choice was available. Both appeared to contain what looks like a unique identifier.

2. The value of _ga, an identifier unique to this browser, was sent to doubleclick.net and google.co.uk in the request address before any consent choice. This appears to allow Google to recognise the browser on later visits.

3. Our review suggests this conflicts with the wording in your privacy policy, which states: “The cookies collect information in an anonymous form, including the number of visitors to the site, where visitors have come to the site from and the pages they visited. This information cannot be used to identify who you are.” The audit observed a unique _ga identifier being sent to Google advertising domains before any consent choice.

4. The privacy policy names 3 companies, but the audit observed Microsoft and found no mention of it by name. I appreciate the policy may refer to some recipients only by category.

5. Our review suggests the international transfer information is incomplete. The policy says Google stores cookie information on servers in the United States, but does not explain the safeguard or other legal mechanism relied on for that transfer.

6. Our review also suggests the privacy policy may be missing two items: who is responsible as controller, and the right to complain to the ICO.

Please reply within one month and:

1. Explain each point above.
2. Confirm which cookies and trackers you consider strictly necessary or otherwise exempt, and why.
3. Stop any non-essential cookies or tracking technologies being set, read or used without consent.
4. Confirm what changes you will make to the privacy information, if any.

If this matter is not resolved, it may be raised with the Information Commissioner’s Office.

Yours faithfully,
Joshua Baker
